description: "Use when creating or updating a React or React plus .NET production pipeline for the shared Docker Compose droplet."

# Application Deployment Contract, Version 1

You are working in an APPLICATION repository. Implement its production
container build/deployment using this contract. Do not modify or bootstrap the
shared droplet, invent application definitions in the infrastructure repo, or
change other sites. This file is intentionally self-contained; explicitly attach
it to the agent request, or reference it from this repository's agent guidance.

## First Establish

Inspect the actual package manager/lockfile, Node/.NET versions, frontend output
directory, API project, current routes and persistence. Identify existing test
commands/projects without creating new ones.
Ask only for genuinely missing deployment inputs: stable `SITE_ID`, primary and
optional redirect hostnames, unused loopback ports, frontend public settings,
and required runtime secret names. Never ask for secret VALUES in chat.

Record the decisions and remaining operator steps in a short deployment section
of this application's README. Do not assume that subdomains belong in their
parent hostname's Nginx file. Avoid unrelated application refactors.

## Validation Scope

Keep deployment validation small and proportional to these hobby projects.
Do not add frontend testing frameworks, browser automation, test suites,
coverage gates, .NET test projects or new test infrastructure just to create a
pipeline. Add these only when explicitly requested. Do not remove existing tests
or weaken established checks; reuse runnable, non-interactive checks already in
the repo. Report absent tests as absent, not as successful test runs.

- Frontend: run the production build and existing lint/typecheck/test commands
  where configured. If there is no real test command, skip the test step; do not
  add a framework, placeholder test or dummy passing command.
- .NET: build/publish the actual API. Run `dotnet test` only when the repo contains
  a real test project, targeting those projects or the existing test solution.
  Do not infer tests from the presence of a solution alone. With no test project,
  omit the test step and note that no tests exist; do not scaffold any.
- Deployment: retain working container health probes, configuration validation
  and a few bounded HTTP smoke checks. Use existing tools such as curl/wget and
  Docker, not a new testing framework. No new fixture databases or integration
  harnesses solely to exercise the deployment; reuse existing test fixtures if
  available, otherwise rely on the host's readiness checks for real dependencies.

Application tests check behavior, not security by themselves. Keep the separate
security controls below (secret handling, image scanning, non-root execution,
loopback-only ports and SSH verification); reducing test scaffolding does not
remove those controls.

## Host Contract

- Ubuntu 26.04 LTS x86-64, current Docker Engine and Compose v2 plugin. Images
  target `linux/amd64`; no builds, SDKs, Node servers or source checkout on host.
- Host Nginx handles public 80/443 and TLS; Certbot uses provider-independent
  HTTP-01 webroot validation. The operator points DNS at the droplet manually
  before first deployment; no DNS API credentials are needed. App containers
  have no public ports or TLS private keys.
- App ID is `[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,39}`, identical to its Compose project name.
- Reserve unique host ports in `18000-18999` in this repo, typically a web/API
  pair. Only publish `127.0.0.1:HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT`. The server rejects
  conflicts with other active projects.
- Runtime secrets: `/etc/sites/SITE_ID/runtime.env`, root-only, operator supplied.
  No application may change shared infrastructure or shared credentials.
- Production CI is trusted with root-equivalent deployment permissions. Do not
  deploy untrusted branches, forks or pull-request code using production secrets.

## Repository Outputs

Generate/adapt `.github/workflows/deploy.yml`, `.dockerignore`, Dockerfiles,
`deploy/compose.yaml`, `deploy/manifest.json`, and
`deploy/nginx/<fully-qualified-hostname>.conf` for EVERY hostname. Container web
server configuration belongs in this repo too. Generate a non-secret runtime
env example listing required variable names if an API needs it.

The workflow assembles this exact release bundle (not source code):

```text
compose.yaml
manifest.json
images.env
nginx/
  www.example.com.conf
```

Both application shapes use the frontend hostname's Nginx file; a .NET API adds
`/api/` routing in that file, not an API hostname or certificate. Frontend-only
deployments omit the API service/image. `images.env` is
generated by CI, not committed. Its only contents are uppercase `*_IMAGE`
assignments containing OCI image digests, e.g.
`WEB_IMAGE=ghcr.io/owner/repository-web@sha256:<64-hex-digest>`.
No comments, tags-only references, `SITE_ID` assignment or secrets in that file.

`deploy/manifest.json` uses schema 1:

```json
{
  "schema": 1,
  "site": "example",
  "domains": ["www.example.com"],
  "ports": [18080, 18081],
  "checks": [
    { "url": "https://www.example.com/", "status": 200 },
    { "url": "https://www.example.com/api/health", "status": 200 }
  ]
}
```

Use actual project values, no unresolved placeholders. Declare all and only
Compose-published ports, and at least one successful HTTPS GET per hostname.
For redirects, add a health location returning 200 so that hostname has a
non-redirecting check as well as its separately tested redirect behavior.
No credentials or nonstandard HTTPS ports in check URLs.
For frontend-only sites remove the API port and `/api/health` check, retaining
the frontend hostname and root check.

## Images And Compose

Use multi-stage builds. Pin upstream base images by digest; automate updates.
Lock dependencies and use `npm ci`/the repo's equivalent. Run only the build and
existing checks described in Validation Scope before publishing.
Exclude `.git`, local env files, build caches and secrets from build contexts.
Do not pass secrets through build args. Prefer dependency caching and GH Actions
build caches rather than downloading tools on the droplet.

**React only:** compile assets in a Node build stage. Serve output on port 8080
using an unprivileged Nginx runtime image, not `npm start` or a development server.
Use an SPA fallback only for navigation routes. Missing assets must return 404,
not HTML; cache hashed assets immutably and do not permanently cache index.html.
Include an unauthenticated `/healthz` endpoint and working image-local probe.
For apps with an API, use a relative `/api/` base URL in browser requests rather
than a hardcoded API origin. Configure a development-server `/api/` proxy to the
local backend, preserving the prefix. Any other public frontend settings use
the app's actual build configuration mechanism; all values embedded in browser
JavaScript are PUBLIC.

**React + .NET:** use the same web image plus an API image built with the
project's supported SDK and matching ASP.NET runtime. Framework-dependent
publish is normally sufficient inside the runtime image. Run as non-root UID
1654 (or the supported image's explicit non-root UID), listen on 8080, and
include a real probe executable in the runtime image. Do not assume curl exists
in Microsoft's runtime image. API readiness must fail when essential database
or schema dependencies are unavailable; liveness need not depend on them.
The backend itself owns the `/api` route prefix, including `/api/health` for
readiness. Use the application's controller routes or route groups consistently;
do not rely on Nginx stripping or adding the prefix, and avoid doubling it.

A representative Compose shape follows. Adapt values, remove `api` for a
frontend-only site, and include a working equivalent of these probes in images:

```yaml
services:
  web:
    image: ${WEB_IMAGE:?required}
    user: "101:101"
    restart: unless-stopped
    init: true
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:18080:8080"
    mem_limit: 64m
    cpus: 0.50
    pids_limit: 100
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=16m,mode=1777
    healthcheck:
      test: [CMD, wget, --spider, -q, http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 6
      start_period: 10s
  api:
    image: ${API_IMAGE:?required}
    user: "1654:1654"
    restart: unless-stopped
    init: true
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:18081:8080"
    env_file:
      - /etc/sites/${SITE_ID:?required}/runtime.env
    environment:
      ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT: Production
      ASPNETCORE_HTTP_PORTS: "8080"
    mem_limit: 384m
    cpus: 0.75
    pids_limit: 200
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=32m,mode=1777
    healthcheck:
      test:
        [
          CMD,
          curl,
          --fail,
          --silent,
          --max-time,
          "3",
          http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/health,
        ]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 6
      start_period: 20s
```

The web image must support UID 101, read-only configuration and PID/cache paths
under `/tmp`; configure these explicitly and test its startup/entrypoint. The API
example assumes curl was explicitly installed into its image. Do not copy probe
commands without verifying tools, writable paths, host filtering and responses.
If health checks require an allowed Host header, include it in the probe.

Use service-local memory/CPU/PID limits as shown, not Swarm-only assumptions.
Start near these memory budgets but measure real workloads; do not promise they
fit 2 GB regardless of app count. Shared CPU limits can sum above one core, but
measure real usage and tune limits without adding a load-testing framework.
Leave host memory headroom. No host networking,
privileged containers, capability additions, arbitrary bind mounts or Docker
socket. Prefer read-only filesystems; explicitly document necessary exceptions.

Use Compose-managed named volumes only for actual persistent uploads/key rings.
Keep volume names stable across releases and attach them in the correct service.
Do not store durable data in a container's writable layer. Persist .NET Data
Protection keys where authentication requires continuity and protect them at
rest. Never run `down -v`, volume prune, or global image/system prune in CI.

## Routing

One file per **exact hostname**, named `<hostname>.conf`, containing only that
hostname's HTTP/HTTPS server blocks. React and its .NET API share that hostname
and file: `/api/` goes to the API container, other paths to the web container.
Unrelated sites/subdomains still get separate files. No wildcard `server_name`, `default_server`,
unrelated aliases, cross-project includes, PHP handlers or app TLS automation.
If an alias must redirect, give it its own file and certificate.

For a React + .NET site at `www.example.com`, the outer host Nginx file is:

```nginx
server {
    listen 80;
    listen [::]:80;
    server_name www.example.com;
    include /etc/nginx/snippets/site-acme.conf;
    location / {
      return 308 https://www.example.com$request_uri;
    }
}
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    listen [::]:443 ssl;
    server_name www.example.com;
    ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/www.example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/www.example.com/privkey.pem;
    include /etc/nginx/snippets/site-tls.conf;
    location = /api {
      return 308 /api/$is_args$args;
    }
    location ^~ /api/ {
      include /etc/nginx/snippets/site-proxy.conf;
      proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:18081;
    }
    location / {
        include /etc/nginx/snippets/site-proxy.conf;
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:18080;
    }
}
```

Every hostname's HTTP block, including redirects/legacy aliases, must include
`site-acme.conf`. Keep the HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect inside `location /`, not at
server scope, so it does not preempt `/.well-known/acme-challenge/`. The shared
snippet serves Certbot's `/var/www/letsencrypt` webroot. No app-container ACME
handler or DNS automation is needed; public port 80 stays open for renewals.

Same-origin `/api/` with prefix preservation is the standard, not an optional
alternative. `proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:18081;` has NO trailing slash:
`/api/users?active=true` must reach .NET unchanged. Do not use the trailing-slash
form that strips `/api/`. The exact `/api` redirect preserves the method via
308 and retains the query string. API 404/errors must remain API responses,
never fall through to the React SPA. Frontend-only sites replace both API
locations with explicit 404 responses rather than proxying to a nonexistent API.

When migrating, change frontend URLs, backend routes, readiness probes and tests
together in THIS application's repo. Inventory external consumers, OAuth
callbacks and cookies before retiring an old API hostname or prefix-stripping
behavior. If temporary compatibility is required, document its removal plan;
any legacy hostname still gets its own file/certificate, never a new default.

Include API readiness in manifest checks even though the hostname already has
a frontend check. Test bare `/api` (308, method and query preserved), `/api/health`,
unknown API routes (404, not SPA HTML), query strings, deep links, missing static
assets, redirects and any WebSockets,
SSE, upload size or timeouts the app uses. Configure security headers appropriate
to this application; do not introduce blanket CSP/HSTS `includeSubDomains`
policies that break unrelated hosts. Enable HSTS after HTTPS cutover is stable.

For .NET configure forwarded headers BEFORE HTTPS redirects/authentication, and
trust only the actual proxy/network path (host Nginx through Docker's bridge).
Recent ASP.NET versions ignore forwarded headers from unknown proxies. Do not
clear KnownProxies/KnownNetworks to trust everyone. Choose an explicit stable
project bridge subnet only if needed for narrow proxy trust, check it does not
overlap the host/VPC/other projects, and test the observed source address. Set
AllowedHosts and HTTPS cookie/redirect behavior. Same-origin browser calls need
no CORS policy; do not add permissive CORS to solve routing errors. Only retain
narrow CORS rules for explicitly required, documented cross-origin consumers.
Test authentication, cookie paths and authorization under `/api/`.

## GitHub Actions Responsibilities

Generate a real workflow suited to THIS repo, not a placeholder. Pin external
actions to reviewed full commit SHAs. Use a protected `production` environment,
deploy only the production branch or explicitly approved dispatch, and set
workflow concurrency per site with `cancel-in-progress: false`. Never use
`pull_request_target` to deploy PR code. Bound job/SSH execution timeouts.

1. Checkout and install the repo's required SDKs. Build the frontend and, when
   present, build/publish the API. Reuse existing lint/typecheck/test commands;
   run `dotnet test` only for existing test projects. Missing tests do not block
   deployment and must not trigger new frameworks, test projects or dummy tests.
   Do not silently skip existing runnable checks or build the same output twice
   without a concrete reason (e.g. image packaging needs a different target).
2. Build one web image and, if applicable, one API image for `linux/amd64`.
   Login to GHCR with `GITHUB_TOKEN`, granting only `contents: read` and
   `packages: write` to the publishing job. Use lowercase GHCR repository names.
   Push unique release tags; capture EACH build action's digest. Do not deploy
   `latest`, mutable tags, or a workflow-dispatch string as the image identity.
3. Validate built image/Compose settings and use a short startup/HTTP smoke check
   where it can run without adding test infrastructure. For a static web image,
   check readiness, a real page/deep link and a missing asset with curl/wget;
   do not install a browser or frontend test runner. For an API, reuse existing
   fixtures if available; otherwise leave dependency-backed readiness to the
   host deployment rather than creating fixture services or injecting production
   credentials into CI. Always keep the host's health/HTTPS checks and resource
   limits. No coverage gate or new application test suite is required. Run a
   vulnerability scan; block fixable high/critical vulnerabilities or record
   reviewed, time-bounded exceptions. Preserve build provenance/SBOM support.
4. Set `RELEASE_ID=${GITHUB_SHA}-${GITHUB_RUN_ID}-${GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT}`. Assemble
   exactly the bundle above; use digests to generate `images.env`. Do not upload
   a tarball, app source, `.git`, secrets or symlinks. Verify manifest/Compose
   hostnames and ports agree. Interpolate only image variables and `SITE_ID` in
   Compose; environment-specific runtime secrets use the server's env file.
5. Configure OpenSSH using `DEPLOY_SSH_KEY` and `DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS` secrets.
   `DEPLOY_HOST` is the droplet IP, not an application's DNS name during cutover.
   Use user `deploy`, port 22, private key mode 0600, SSH directory mode 0700,
   `BatchMode=yes`, `IdentitiesOnly=yes`, `StrictHostKeyChecking=yes`, explicit
   known-hosts file and connection timeout. Never disable host checking or
   blindly run ssh-keyscan; never print private keys/tokens. Pass secrets through
   step environment variables, not shell interpolation of GitHub expressions.
6. Validate the slug/release ID before constructing remote commands. Create
   `/srv/deploy/incoming/$SITE_ID/$RELEASE_ID/` as `deploy` with mode 0700 using
   SSH. SCP `compose.yaml`, `manifest.json`, `images.env` and the `nginx/`
   directory into it, preserving the exact layout. Deploy only once upload is
   complete. Prefer direct SSH/SCP over a third-party SSH action.
7. Invoke the ONLY sudo deployment command:

   ```bash
   sudo -n /usr/local/sbin/site-deploy apply SITE_ID RELEASE_ID --public
   ```

   Build the optional flag from `vars.DEPLOY_PUBLIC_CHECKS`: require an explicit
   `true` or `false`; append `--public` only for `true`. Use `true` for initial
   and normal deployments. `false` is explicit diagnostic mode only: it skips
   public smoke checks, not ACME validation. Fresh issuance still needs public
   DNS pointing here and port 80 reachable. Local TLS/routing checks always run.
   Quote validated arguments, propagate remote exit status, and do
   not run `docker compose` directly as `deploy`.

8. For normal deployments, also perform an external HTTPS smoke test from the
   GitHub runner, plus project-specific checks (API paths, expected health JSON,
   redirects, authentication where safe). Skip public-DNS tests ONLY in the
   explicit diagnostic mode. If a post-activation check fails, invoke:

   ```bash
   sudo -n /usr/local/sbin/site-deploy rollback SITE_ID RELEASE_ID --public
   ```

   This refuses a stale rollback if another release is current. Do not invoke
   it after an `apply` failure, since the helper already attempts recovery.
   Surface rollback failures and keep the workflow failed after recovery.

The helper serializes host changes, validates resolved Compose policy, refuses
hostname/port collisions or unmanaged route overwrites, pulls images, obtains
missing per-host certificates, waits for healthy containers, installs routes,
runs `nginx -t`/reload, checks HTTPS and only then promotes `current`/`previous`.
Initial HTTP-01 issuance uses the shared HTTP listener before app routes exist.
Do not install TLS routes referring to nonexistent certificates or claim that
disabling public smoke checks permits pre-DNS certificate issuance.
It retains failed bundles and never deletes persistent volumes. Recreate/update
uses a stable project name; short downtime is expected. No SDK/build workloads
or per-app systemd units belong on the droplet. Keep logs free of resolved Compose
secret values; do not print `docker compose config` with production env files.

## Persistence, Migrations And Handoff

Inventory uploads, scheduled workers, external storage, API paths and key rings.
External databases require droplet allowlisting and verified TLS. Do not run
destructive migrations automatically on API startup. Prefer backward-compatible
expand/contract schema changes and a deliberate, idempotent migration stage;
decide where it runs and how it authenticates before implementing it. If no safe
automated migration path exists, explicitly document the operator gate. Image
rollback does not reverse schema changes or restore data/secrets.

Document only unavoidable manual steps: choose hostnames/ports, populate
production environment secrets (`DEPLOY_HOST`, `DEPLOY_SSH_KEY`,
`DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS`), set `DEPLOY_PUBLIC_CHECKS`, authorize package pulls for the
host registry identity, populate `/etc/sites/SITE_ID/runtime.env` if needed,
allowlist external services, migrate persistent data and perform DNS cutover.
Prepare/test images before cutover; the operator points A/AAAA records using the
DNS provider's interface and waits for propagation before initial deployment.
Allow a first-cutover outage while issuance and startup complete. Keep stale
AAAA records and CDN/proxy interception from breaking HTTP validation. DNS must
continue resolving here for automatic renewal; no DNS token belongs on the host.
Host provisioning, GHCR login and backups are shared operator duties;
no copies of those credentials or bootstrap logic in this repo's pipeline.

Finish by running the build, existing runnable checks, lightweight smoke checks
and workflow/config validation within Validation Scope. Do not create extra
test tooling to satisfy this handoff. Distinguish local/CI validation from a real droplet
deployment; never claim live TLS, firewall, DNS or rollback success without
actually testing them. State any remaining migration or verification gates.
